questions.question:
Which of the following idioms given in the alternatives has the meaning?
A person who is strong, resilient, and not easily defeated or discouraged in difficult situations.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is: **Option 1 i.e. Tough cookie**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The idiom **"Tough cookie"** refers to a person who is strong, resilient, and not easily discouraged, especially in difficult situations. (हिम्मत वाला व्यक्ति)
 
 
• **Example:** Despite losing several matches, she proved to be a tough cookie and eventually won the championship.
 
 
• The idiom highlights strength of character, determination, and the ability to face adversity with courage.

Therefore, the correct answer is: **Tough cookie**.

---

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

Here are the other options explained along with their Hindi meanings and example sentences:

 
• **Tough cheese** (दुर्भाग्य): This is a sarcastic phrase used to indicate "too bad" or "unlucky" in an unsympathetic way. 
 
 
• **Example:** "You missed the bus? Tough cheese, you’ll have to wait for the next one."
 
 

 
• **Tough sledding** (कठिनाई): This idiom refers to difficult progress or challenges in achieving something. 
 
 
• **Example:** "It was tough sledding for the team as they tried to climb the ranks in the league."
 
 

 
• **Tough row to hoe** (मुश्किल काम): This idiom describes a difficult task or challenge that one must handle. 
 
 
• **Example:** "Starting a business in this economy is a tough row to hoe."

questions.question:

questions.question:
Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Passive Voice?

We were rearranging the library when the earthquake occurred.

options.text: The library was rearranged by us when the earthquake occurred.
The library were rearranged by us when the earthquake occurred.
When the earthquake occurred, we were rearranging the library.
The library was being rearranged by us when the earthquake occurred.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 4**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Identify the Tense:** The main clause "We were rearranging the library" is in the **Past Continuous Tense** (Subject + was/were + $V_1$ + ing + Object).
 
• **Passive Voice Structure (Past Continuous):** The rule for converting past continuous active to passive is: *Object + was/were + **being** + $V_3$ (past participle) + by + Subject.*
 
• **Subject-Verb Agreement:** The new subject "The library" is singular, so we must use the auxiliary verb **"was."**
 
• **Verb Form:** The continuous nature of the action is maintained by adding **"being,"** followed by the past participle of the main verb, **"rearranged."**
 
• **Time Clause:** The secondary clause "when the earthquake occurred" describes the background event and remains unchanged in the passive conversion.

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 4**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"The library was being rearranged by us when the earthquake occurred."*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1: **"The library was rearranged..." – Incorrect because it uses the **Simple Past** passive form, which fails to convey the ongoing action of the original sentence.
 
• **Option 2: **"The library were rearranged..." – Incorrect because "library" is a singular subject and requires "was," and it also omits the "being" required for continuous tenses.
 
• **Option 3: **"When the earthquake occurred, we were rearranging..." – Incorrect because the sentence is still in the **Active Voice**; only the order of the clauses has been changed.

questions.question:
Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Passive Voice?

Are the scientists developing a new medicine for the disease?

options.text: Has a new medicine for the disease been developed by the scientists?
Is a new medicine for the disease being developed by the scientists?
Was a new medicine for the disease being developed by the scientists?
Is a new medicine for the disease developed by the scientists?

questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 2**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Identify the Tense:** The active sentence "Are the scientists developing...?" is in the **Present Continuous Tense** (is/am/are + $V_1$ + ing).
 
• **Passive Voice Structure (Present Continuous Interrogative):** The structure for questions is: *Is/Am/Are + Object + **being** + $V_3$ (past participle) + by + Subject?*
 
• **Subject-Verb Agreement:** The object "a new medicine for the disease" is singular, so the auxiliary verb **"Is"** is correctly used at the beginning.
 
• **The "Being" Component:** To maintain the continuous nature of the action in passive voice, the word **"being"** must be used before the past participle.
 
• **Verb Form:** The main verb "developing" changes to its past participle form, **"developed."**

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 2**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"Is a new medicine for the disease being developed by the scientists?"*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1: **"Has... been developed" – Incorrect because it changes the tense to **Present Perfect**.
 
• **Option 3: **"Was... being developed" – Incorrect because it changes the tense to **Past Continuous**.
 
• **Option 4: **"Is... developed" – Incorrect because it uses the **Simple Present** passive form, missing the "being" required for continuous actions.

questions.question:
Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into active voice?

Where was the meeting held by the union leaders?

options.text: Where did the union leaders hold the meeting?
Where had the union leaders held the meeting?
Where have the union leaders held the meeting?
Where do the union leaders hold the meeting?

questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 1**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Identify the Tense:** The passive sentence "Where was the meeting held by the union leaders?" is in the **Simple Past Tense** (Interrogative form).
 
• **Passive to Active Structure:** The passive structure *"Wh-word + was/were + Object + V3 + by + Subject?"* converts to the active structure: **"Wh-word + did + Subject + V1 + Object?"**
 
• **Identify Subject and Object:** In the passive sentence, the agent is "the union leaders" (Subject) and the receiver of the action is "the meeting" (Object).
 
• **Verb Change:** The past participle "held" (V3) changes to the base form **"hold"** (V1) because the auxiliary verb "did" is used to indicate the past tense in active interrogative sentences.

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 1**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"Where did the union leaders hold the meeting?"*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 2: **"Where had the union leaders held..." – Incorrect because it uses the **Past Perfect Tense**.
 
• **Option 3: **"Where have the union leaders held..." – Incorrect because it uses the **Present Perfect Tense**.
 
• **Option 4: **"Where do the union leaders hold..." – Incorrect because it uses the **Simple Present Tense**.

questions.question:
Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into active voice?

Had the final draft of the proposal been prepared by the secretary before the deadline?

options.text: Did the secretary prepare the final draft of the proposal before the deadline?
Has the secretary prepared the final draft of the proposal before the deadline?
Had the secretary prepared the final draft of the proposal before the deadline?
Was the secretary preparing the final draft of the proposal before the deadline?

questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 3**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Identify the Tense:** The sentence "Had the final draft... been prepared...?" is in the **Past Perfect Tense** (Interrogative form).
 
• **Passive to Active Structure:** The passive structure *"Had + Object + been + $V_3$ + by + Subject?"* converts to the active structure: **"Had + Subject + $V_3$ + Object?"**
 
• **Identify Subject and Object:** In the passive voice, the agent (the one doing the action) is "the secretary." In the active voice, this agent becomes the subject. The receiver, "the final draft of the proposal," becomes the object.
 
• **Verb Form:** The auxiliary verb "Had" remains unchanged, and the past participle ($V_3$) form "prepared" is used in both active and passive for the Past Perfect tense.

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 3**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"Had the secretary prepared the final draft of the proposal before the deadline?"*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **Option 4: **"Was the secretary preparing..." – Incorrect because it changes the tense to **Past Continuous**.

questions.question:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.
S1. When Kavery reached the field she grinned to herself.
A. She worked hard in the field for the next few months and managed to grow a good crop.
B. All she needed to do now was sow the seeds.
C. Just as she had expected, the thief had spent the night digging up the land nicely for her.
D. She sold those and finally they had some money.
S2. With a part of this money Kavery bought some jewellery.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 4**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• The paragraph begins with S1, where Kavery reaches the field and grins, setting the stage for the subsequent events.
 
• **Sentence C comes first** as it explains the reason for Kavery's grin, revealing that the thief had unknowingly done the hard work of digging the land for her:
 
 
• "Just as she had expected, the thief had spent the night digging up the land nicely for her."
 
 
• **Sentence B follows** as it logically describes the next step in the sequence—Kavery sowing the seeds:
 
 
• "All she needed to do now was sow the seeds."
 
 
• **Sentence A comes third** as it depicts her hard work in the field and the result of growing a good crop:
 
 
• "She worked hard in the field for the next few months and managed to grow a good crop."
 
 
• **Sentence D is the fourth** as it concludes the chain of events, showing how Kavery sold the crop and earned money:
 
 
• "She sold those and finally they had some money."
 
 
• The paragraph ends with S2, where Kavery uses part of the money to buy some jewelry, providing closure to the story.

 

**Correct sequence:** CBAD

 

**Coherent paragraph after rearrangement:**

"When Kavery reached the field she grinned to herself. Just as she had expected, the thief had spent the night digging up the land nicely for her. All she needed to do now was sow the seeds. She worked hard in the field for the next few months and managed to grow a good crop. She sold those and finally they had some money. With a part of this money Kavery bought some jewellery."

questions.question: What were the reasons for the establishment of 'The Movement' group in Britain?

options.text: The oppositions were against the cultural pretensions and elitism of the Bloomsbury and Bohemian groups
Modernist elitism was advocated, and experimental writing styles were in the limelight
Romantic ideals were revived, and irony in poetry was completely rejected
Avant-garde art and radical political movements were encouraged instead

questions.solution:
The correct answer is '**Option 1**'.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• ***Option 1: The oppositions were against the cultural pretensions and elitism of the Bloomsbury and Bohemian groups.***

 
 
• **The Movement** was a term coined in 1954 to describe a group of British writers (including Philip Larkin and Kingsley Amis) who rejected the high-flown, "intellectual" elitism of the **Bloomsbury Group** and the earlier **Bohemian** lifestyle.
 
• They stood for **anti-pretentiousness** and

questions.question: Who coined the term 'The Movement'?

options.text: Kingsley Amis, one of the leading novelists of the group
J. D. Scott, literary editor of The Spectator
Donald Davie, poet-critic and member of the group
Robert Conquest, known for his satirical verses

questions.solution:
The correct answer is '**Option 2**'.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• ***Option 2: J. D. Scott, literary editor of The Spectator.***

 
 
• The term **"The Movement"** was officially coined by **J. D. Scott** in an anonymous leading article titled **"In the Movement"** published in *The Spectator* on October 1, 1954.
 
• In the article, Scott identified a new group of British writers who shared a common skepticism toward the high-modernist and romantic styles of the previous decades.
 
• He described their work as being characterized by **"anti-phoneyism,"** technical proficiency, and a rejection of the "bloated" or "pretentious" language found in the works of Dylan Thomas or the Bloomsbury Group.
 
 
 
• ***Option 1: Kingsley Amis...***
 
 
• This is **incorrect**. While Amis was a central figure and his novel *Lucky Jim* (1954) is seen as a foundational text of the group, he did not name the movement himself.
 
 
 
• ***Option 3: Donald Davie...***
 
 
• This is **incorrect**. Davie was a key poet and critic associated with the group (especially through his work *Purity of Diction in English Verse*), but he was a participant rather than the coiner of the name.
 
 
 
• ***Option 4: Robert Conquest...***
 
 
• This is **incorrect**. Conquest edited the famous anthology ***New Lines* (1956)**, which crystallized the group's identity, but J. D. Scott had already coined the term in the press two years earlier.
 
 

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 2.**

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Historical Context**: The Movement emerged in the post-WWII era, reflecting a period of austerity and a shift toward the "Angry Young Men" sentiment in British culture.
 
• **Anti-Romanticism**: The group was largely defined by what they were *against*: the excessive emotion of Romanticism and the difficult, elitist obscurity of Modernism.
 
• **Key Contributors**: Along with Philip Larkin and Kingsley Amis, the group included John Wain, Elizabeth Jennings, Thom Gunn, and D. J. Enright. Their work often featured **irony**, **common sense**, and **traditional verse forms**.

questions.question: How were The Movement writers often identified socially and culturally?

options.text: By their aristocratic background and preference for the elite salon
Through their working-class origins and radical political activism
Through their connection with cosmopolitan intellectual circles and experimental art
Through their middle-class roots, beer-drinking, and pipe-smoking habits

questions.solution:
The correct answer is '**Option 4**'.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• ***Option 4: Through their middle-class roots, beer-drinking, and pipe-smoking habits.***

 
 
• **The Movement** writers were often identified with a distinctly **middle-class, provincial** background. They were frequently scholarship boys from grammar schools who felt alienated from the upper-class "metropolitan" elite.
 
• Culturally, they adopted a persona of the **"plain man."** This was famously symbolized by their preference for **beer and pipes** over the wine and experimental drugs associated with previous avant-garde or "Bohemian" circles.
 
• They took pride in being **anti-intellectual** in their public image—though they were highly educated—to signal their rejection of what they called "phoney" or "posh" artistic pretensions.
 
 
 
• ***Option 1: Aristocratic background and elite salons...***
 
 
• This is **incorrect**. This describes the **Bloomsbury Group** (e.g., Virginia Woolf), whom The Movement writers actively despised for their perceived elitism and "high-brow" aesthetic.
 
 
 
• ***Option 2: Working-class origins and radical activism...***
 
 
• This is **incorrect**. While they shared some "grumpy" energy with the working-class *Angry Young Men*, most Movement writers (like Larkin and Amis) were firmly **middle-class** and generally held skeptical, conservative, or moderate political views.
 
 
 
• ***Option 3: Cosmopolitan intellectual circles and experimental art...***
 
 
• This is **incorrect**. The Movement was **anti-cosmopolitan** and **anti-experimental**. They preferred a local, traditional English focus over international modernism.
 
 

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 4.**

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **The "Plain Man" Aesthetic**: This was a deliberate cultural performance. By appearing as ordinary men who liked jazz, beer, and detective novels, they made poetry seem like a practical, "honest" craft rather than a mystical or elite calling.
 
• **Anti-Phoneyism**: A term popularized by the group (and J.D. Salinger around the same time) to describe their hatred for anything that seemed fake, overly sentimental, or intellectually arrogant.
 
• **Larkin and the Library**: Philip Larkin’s career as a librarian in Hull perfectly exemplified this "Movement" identity—working a steady, middle-class job in a provincial city while writing poetry that was technically masterful but grounded in everyday observation.

questions.question: What attitude did The Movement writers share toward modernist literature?

options.text: They appreciated its intricacy and sought to experiment likewise through their writing.
They looked down upon its elitist nature and cultural pretensions, choosing clarity and accessibility in writing
They accepted the use of avant-garde techniques and denounced the English identity based on tradition.
They turned away from irony and nostalgia, concentrating exclusively on abstract philosophical discussions

questions.solution:
The correct answer is '**Option 2**'.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• ***Option 2: They looked down upon its elitist nature and cultural pretensions, choosing clarity and accessibility in writing.***

 
 
• **The Movement** writers (such as Philip Larkin and Kingsley Amis) were defined by their reaction **against** the "difficulty" and obscurity of High Modernism (represented by T.S. Eliot and Ezra Pound).
 
• They felt that Modernism had become too **elitist** and disconnected from the ordinary reader. In response, they championed **"anti-phoneyism"**—a rejection of anything that seemed intellectually arrogant or overly complex.
 
• They prioritized **clarity**, **logic**, and **accessibility**, believing that literature should be grounded in the observable world rather than in abstract myths or private symbols.
 
 
 
• ***Option 1: They appreciated its intricacy and sought to experiment...***
 
 
• This is **incorrect**. The group viewed Modernist experimentation as a "dead end" and preferred to return to **traditional English verse forms** like the sonnet or quatrain.
 
 
 
• ***Option 3: They accepted the use of avant-garde techniques...***
 
 
• This is **incorrect**. They were famously suspicious of the **avant-garde**, which they associated with foreign (non-English) influences that they felt didn't fit the British temperament.
 
 
 
• ***Option 4: They turned away from irony and nostalgia...***
 
 
• This is **incorrect**. Irony and a certain gritty nostalgia for a passing version of England were actually **central** to their style. They avoided "abstract philosophical discussions" in favor of concrete, everyday details.
 
 

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 2.**

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Rationalism over Romanticism**: The Movement writers valued the intellect over the "wild" emotions of the Romantics and the "stream-of-consciousness" confusion of the Modernists.
 
• **The "Grammar School" Poets**: Because many of them were educated in provincial grammar schools rather than the aristocratic circles of the Bloomsbury Group, their attitude toward Modernism was one of **middle-class skepticism** toward "high-brow" culture.
 
• **Philip Larkin's Prefaces**: Larkin often wrote about how he wanted poetry to be something people actually *wanted* to read, famously stating that he had no interest in "any poetry that requires a notebook of cross-references to understand."
